edits.why_correct: A well patient with a new fever in hospital, a relatively slow pulse, eosinophilia, and no source on a thorough infection screen suggests a drug reaction. Allopurinol is a recognised cause of drug fever and of DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms), and omeprazole has no clear indication, so both new medicines should be stopped. Fever with eosinophilia after starting allopurinol can be an early hypersensitivity reaction before any rash appears, so monitoring the temperature alone is not enough: he needs a clinical reassessment of skin, mucous membranes, lymph nodes and observations, and repeat blood tests including full blood count and film, liver function, renal function and urinalysis to look for organ involvement. Escalate to a senior and dermatology if a rash, rising eosinophils or organ involvement develops, and report the reaction via the Yellow Card scheme. Simple drug fever usually settles within about 48–72 hours of stopping the culprit. Source: DermNet Drug hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS); Pyrexia of unknown origin, Patient.info professional reference (reviewed 2024); Investigating and managing pyrexia of unknown origin in adults, BMJ, 2010.

Bone marrow examination is invasive and premature when stopping the probable culprit drugs has not yet been tried. E. A 38-year-old woman has had fevers of up to 38.6°C on most days for 4 weeks, with fatigue and 3 kg weight loss. She is haemodynamically stable, eating and drinking. A detailed history and repeated examination have found no focus, and there is no heart murmur. Full blood count shows haemoglobin 108 g/L with normal white cells and platelets. C-reactive protein is 62 mg/L. Urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, thyroid function, urinalysis and urine culture, three sets of blood cultures, HIV test, autoimmune screen and chest X-ray are normal or negative. She has no recent travel.

Which is the most appropriate next step?
edits.why_correct: She now meets the definition of classical pyrexia of unknown origin and is stable, with a raised C-reactive protein. The history, repeated examination, baseline blood tests and microbiology have been completed and give no clue to direct a specific test, so the most useful next step is cross-sectional imaging of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, chosen to look for occult infection (such as an abscess), malignancy (such as lymphoma or a solid tumour) or inflammatory disease, which then directs further tests. In other patients the next test is guided by any clinical clues, and FDG-PET-CT may follow if CT does not help. Empirical antibiotics and steroids are avoided in stable patients because they can mask the cause and delay diagnosis. Source: Investigating and managing pyrexia of unknown origin in adults, BMJ, 2010; Pyrexia of unknown origin, Patient.info professional reference (reviewed 2024).

edits.stem:
A 36-year-old man is admitted after his family find him neglecting himself. Over the past three months he has had very low mood, early morning waking, poor appetite with 6 kg weight loss, and loss of interest in everything. Starting in the same week as the low mood and continuing throughout, he has believed that a government agency inserts thoughts into his head, and he hears two voices discussing him in the third person. He was treated with an antidepressant and an antipsychotic. His mood has now been normal for four weeks, with normal sleep and appetite, but the voices and thought insertion continue unchanged. He has never had a manic episode, and there is no substance misuse.

Using ICD-11, what is the most likely diagnosis?
edits.why_correct: ICD-11, the WHO classification used for diagnosis in UK practice, defines schizoaffective disorder as an episode in which the requirements for schizophrenia and for a moderate or severe depressive (or manic or mixed) episode are met in the same episode of illness, simultaneously or within a few days of each other, with symptoms lasting at least one month. He had a severe depressive episode and, starting in the same week, two core schizophrenia symptoms (thought insertion, a passivity experience, and third-person auditory hallucinations) for three months. His psychosis then continued after his mood recovered, which argues against psychotic depression, where psychotic symptoms are confined to the depressive episode. (The US DSM-5-TR also requires at least two weeks of psychosis without a mood episode, which he would also meet.) Source: WHO ICD-11 6A21 Schizoaffective disorder (MMS v2026-01).
edits.pearl: Schizophrenia-type symptoms and a full mood episode in the same episode of illness = schizoaffective disorder (ICD-11); psychosis that outlasts the mood episode points away from psychotic depression.
edits.thinking: Severe depressive episode for 3 months  ↓  First-rank symptoms (thought insertion, third-person voices) starting the same week, ≥1 month  ↓  ICD-11: schizophrenia and mood requirements met in the same episode  ↓  Psychosis persists after mood recovers; no mania, no substances  ↓  Schizoaffective disorder
edits.takeaway: ICD-11: schizophrenia-type symptoms and a moderate or severe mood episode together in the same episode = schizoaffective disorder.
edits.notes: Framework: ICD-11 (6A21), as used in UK practice. The vignette meets ICD-11 (schizophrenia and severe depressive episode requirements met simultaneously, onset in the same week, >1 month). DSM-5-TR additionally needs >=2 weeks of psychosis without a mood episode; the vignette also meets that, but it is mentioned only as a secondary note. Existing GF028 is a manic (bipolar-type) diagnosis question; this is a case with a depressive episode.
edits.presentation: Schizoaffective disorder — mood and psychotic symptoms in the same episode

edits.stem:
A 33-year-old man has had schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, for six years and is under the care of his community mental health team psychiatrist. He takes lithium, and his plasma lithium level is 0.7 mmol/L. He has had no manic or depressive episode for 10 months, and his mood, sleep and energy are currently normal. However, he continues to hear voices discussing him and believes his neighbours are poisoning his water. He has had two sequential antipsychotic trials, each at an adequate dose for 8 weeks: first risperidone, then aripiprazole. Neither helped, and adherence to both was confirmed by his community nurse. His diagnosis has been reviewed, he does not use alcohol or drugs, and he has completed CBT for psychosis and family intervention.

What is the most appropriate next step in his drug treatment?

options.D: Clozapine, initiated by his psychiatrist, with weekly FBCs

edits.correct_answer: D. Clozapine, initiated by his psychiatrist, with weekly FBCs
edits.why_correct: His mood component is controlled, so the problem is the persistent psychosis. It has not responded to two adequate, sequential antipsychotic trials (adequate dose and duration, adherence confirmed, one a non-clozapine second-generation drug), and other causes of non-response have been reviewed. This is treatment-resistant psychosis, and clozapine should be offered. There is no NICE guideline specifically for schizoaffective disorder; the specialist team applies the schizophrenia guideline to the persistent psychotic component. Clozapine is started and supervised by a specialist, and the patient must be registered with a monitoring service, with a full blood count before starting and at least weekly for the first 18 weeks because of the risk of agranulocytosis. Source: NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults (2014, last updated 2026, recs 1.5.7.1–1.5.7.2); Clozaril SmPC (emc, revised February 2026).
edits.thinking: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type  ↓  Mood stable on therapeutic lithium  ↓  Psychosis persists after two sequential antipsychotic trials at adequate dose and duration (one SGA), adherence confirmed, other causes reviewed  ↓  Treatment-resistant psychosis  ↓  Psychiatrist initiates clozapine with registration and weekly FBC for 18 weeks
edits.takeaway: Psychosis in schizoaffective disorder that fails two adequate, sequential antipsychotic trials: specialist-initiated clozapine with blood monitoring.

edits.stem:
A 34-year-old man is in the intensive care unit 4 days after a motorcycle collision. He had a pelvic fracture and a splenic laceration, needed a splenectomy and received a massive transfusion on the day of injury; he has had no blood products since day 1. He is now intubated, with bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray and a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 18 kPa. His urine output has been under 0.3 mL/kg/hour for 24 hours and his creatinine has risen from 82 to 315 micromol/L, so haemofiltration is being started. His platelet count has fallen to 41 × 10⁹/L and his INR is 2.1. Blood cultures and line-tip cultures are negative and no source of infection has been found.

Which term best describes his condition?
edits.why_correct: Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) is altered function of two or more organ systems in an acutely ill patient, such that homeostasis cannot be maintained without intervention. His respiratory failure needing ventilation and acute kidney injury needing renal replacement already meet this definition, and his low platelets and raised INR show that the haematological system is also affected. This follows the inflammatory 'second hit' of major trauma, massive transfusion and surgery, and is a recognised cause of late death after major trauma. Source: ACCP/SCCM Consensus Conference definitions for sepsis and organ failure (Bone et al., Chest, 1992).
edits.thinking: Major trauma + splenectomy + massive transfusion  ↓  Day 4: ventilated with bilateral infiltrates (lungs)  ↓  Oliguria and rising creatinine needing haemofiltration (kidneys)  ↓  Low platelets and raised INR (clotting also affected)  ↓  Two or more organ systems failing, needing support  ↓  Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome

edits.why_correct: Intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance and arousal starting immediately after an exceptionally threatening event, and already easing day by day while he keeps functioning, fit an acute stress reaction: in ICD-11 this is a transient response to an extreme stressor that is considered normal given its severity and usually begins to subside within a few days. It is not the same as DSM-5 acute stress disorder, which needs at least 9 of 14 specified symptoms lasting from 3 days to 1 month and causing significant distress or impairment; his symptoms are fewer, improving and not disabling. Post-traumatic stress disorder can only be diagnosed when symptoms persist for more than 1 month after the trauma (DSM-5), and NICE structures care in the first month as active monitoring for settling symptoms or early trauma-focused treatment for acute stress disorder, rather than treatment of established PTSD. Source: NICE NG116 Post-traumatic stress disorder, 2018; WHO ICD-11 QE84 Acute stress reaction; DSM-5 criteria for acute stress disorder and PTSD.
edits.pearl: Same symptoms, different clock: PTSD needs more than a month; a settling response in the first days is an acute stress reaction, while marked, persisting symptoms within the month suggest acute stress disorder.

edits.takeaway: Trauma symptoms that settle over the first few days are an acute stress reaction; PTSD needs symptoms persisting beyond a month.

edits.stem:
A 44-year-old woman was the driver in a low-speed rear-end car collision 5 days ago and has had right-sided neck pain since. Yesterday she had 30 minutes of weakness and clumsiness of her left hand, which resolved completely. Her GP gave her aspirin 300 mg straight away and referred her immediately, and she is seen in the TIA clinic today. Examination today is normal apart from a mild right ptosis and a smaller right pupil. MRI of the brain shows no infarct or haemorrhage. CT angiography shows a long, tapering narrowing of the right internal carotid artery starting 2 cm above the bifurcation, consistent with dissection, with about 70% narrowing of the lumen. She takes no regular medicines and has no history of bleeding.

Which is the most appropriate management?
edits.why_correct: NICE advises aspirin 300 mg immediately for suspected TIA unless contraindicated and specialist assessment within 24 hours, and both have been done; the question is the ongoing antithrombotic plan once the cause is known. This is a TIA caused by extracranial internal carotid artery dissection, and the narrowing is due to an intramural haematoma rather than atherosclerotic plaque. UK guidance is to treat ischaemic stroke due to cervical artery dissection with either an anticoagulant or an antiplatelet agent for at least 3 months, with no proven advantage of one over the other; for stroke or TIA due to dissection, dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel may be considered for the first 21 days, followed by antiplatelet monotherapy until at least 3 months after onset. Most dissections heal or recanalise with medical treatment, so surgery is not indicated. Source: National Clinical Guideline for Stroke for the UK and Ireland, Intercollegiate Stroke Working Party, 2023 (section 3.8); NICE NG128 Stroke and TIA in over 16s, 2019 (recs 1.1.4, 1.1.5 and 1.4.14).

edits.notes: Existing DF028 has aspirin as the answer for dissection with an established infarct; this item tests a TIA with high-grade luminal narrowing and the endarterectomy trap, and the answer is the guideline wording (antiplatelet or anticoagulant). NICE NG128 1.4.14 covers stroke; the ICSWP 2023 guideline extends this to TIA (DAPT for 21 days for stroke or TIA). Reviewer (Oct 2026): stem now states immediate aspirin 300 mg and immediate referral (NG128 1.1.4–1.1.5), so the 3-month regimen follows rather than replaces the immediate TIA pathway; consistent with DAPT-for-21-days option in ICSWP.

edits.why_correct: Sudden headache, flushing and sweating above the level of the lesion, a blood pressure more than 20 mmHg above her baseline and a relative bradycardia in someone with a cord injury at T6 or above is autonomic dysreflexia. After sitting the patient up and loosening clothing, the priority is to find and remove the noxious stimulus below the lesion: the bladder is checked first, and when it is excluded, the rectum is gently checked using lidocaine gel, removing any faecal mass. Throughout, she is kept upright and her blood pressure is checked every 2 to 5 minutes, following the local autonomic dysreflexia protocol. If the systolic pressure rises above 150 mmHg at any point, or stays high once the trigger is dealt with, it is treated promptly (for example nifedipine 10 mg bite-and-swallow or a GTN spray) rather than continuing to search for a trigger, with senior and spinal cord injury centre advice if symptoms do not settle quickly. Source: Autonomic dysreflexia guidance, Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital Spinal Cord Injury Centre; Autonomic dysreflexia, British Association of Urological Surgeons.
edits.pearl: In autonomic dysreflexia, think 'sit up, then bladder, then bowel' — check the blood pressure every few minutes and treat it promptly if systolic goes above 150 mmHg.
edits.takeaway: In autonomic dysreflexia, once the bladder is excluded, check the bowel using lidocaine gel while monitoring blood pressure closely.
edits.notes: Existing GF039 tests sit-up-and-check-catheter (bladder trigger, T4). This item deliberately excludes the bladder and tests the next trigger (bowel) at a lower systolic pressure so that drug treatment is not yet indicated (RNOH threshold systolic > 150 mmHg). Reviewer (Oct 2026): RNOH protocol checked — monitor BP every 2–5 minutes; systolic >150 mmHg → immediate nifedipine 10 mg or GTN 1–2 sprays; admit/contact SCI centre if not resolving. Added to explanation.

reviewer_point: Explanation must not imply perimetry alone is enough; a new persistent field loss needs timely assessment and investigation for an intracranial cause.
response: The existing brain-imaging sentence applied only if perimetry confirmed a homonymous defect, so it has been strengthened. why_correct now says perimetry defines the defect but not its cause, and that a new persistent defect needs timely ophthalmic/neurological assessment and neuroimaging, with stroke work-up (including AF), and same-day assessment if onset is sudden or there are other neurological features. The thinking chain and takeaway now carry this too. Source: NHS Scotland Community Eyecare Guideline 12.1 Homonymous hemianopia (management: 'Exclusion of atrial fibrillation', 'If acute, or in the young, specialist vascular evaluation by stroke team', 'Neuroimaging').

edits.why_correct: Confrontation testing is a quick bedside screen, but it is insensitive and cannot map the shape, depth or exact edges of a field defect. Formal perimetry, usually standard automated perimetry (for example Humphrey testing), measures sensitivity at fixed points across the field of each eye and gives a reproducible chart that shows whether a defect is homonymous, respects the vertical midline, or spares the macula, which localises the lesion and allows monitoring. UK practice uses standard automated perimetry for formal field assessment, and the DVLA uses automated binocular (Esterman) field testing for licensing. Perimetry defines the defect but does not explain it, so it is not the end of his care. A new, persistent field loss needs timely ophthalmic or neurological assessment. If perimetry confirms a homonymous defect, as his symptoms suggest, the lesion is behind the optic chiasm and he needs neuroimaging to look for a stroke, tumour or other intracranial cause, with a stroke work-up (including checking for atrial fibrillation) if a vascular cause is likely. Sudden-onset loss or other neurological symptoms would need same-day stroke or emergency assessment. Source: Glaucoma: diagnosis and management, NICE NG81, 2017 (updated 2022); Assessing fitness to drive: visual disorders, DVLA, GOV.UK, current edition; Visual field defect, homonymous hemianopia (Community Eyecare Guideline 12.1), NHS Scotland.

edits.takeaway: Suspected visual field defects are characterised with formal automated perimetry, but a confirmed new defect still needs investigation for its cause, including brain imaging.

edits.why_correct: Acute hypertensive retinal changes such as haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and exudates usually resolve over weeks to months once blood pressure is controlled, and vision is generally preserved. Treatment is control of blood pressure; eye procedures are kept for complications such as macular oedema with visual loss. They also needed active blood pressure treatment rather than reassurance alone, followed by sustained control and repeat fundoscopy.
